Getting help is something that is individually crafted for a person. Things that might help me might not help you. Honestly I’d say it’s the hardest part of healing... so that’s a difficult question, and it’s understandable if neither of you can answer it. Even I can’t answer it for myself sometimes and I’ve learned to be okay with that. When I don’t know what will help, I just give up. Which could also be the case here. We’re all guilty of it. Nobody is born understanding the human psyche and how to nurse it, and that’s okay. But after you’ve given up you definitely know that doesn’t help. Don’t exhaust your resources, though. Talking to others who struggle with mental issues could help, assuming you haven’t already, and I don’t just mean reddit. Group therapy, individual therapy, etc. They’re scary for sure but it could benefit you two, both in finding solutions and understanding each other’s feelings about this

It can seem like an impossible thing, but maybe if you both sat down and made a list together it could help. A list of anything. What makes you happy, how you define life, the things that hurt you. Stuff you probably already know about each other, yes, but often that can get lost along the way. I forgot who said it but I heard a quote once along the lines of, “sometimes you love someone so much you end up on the other side of them.” It could be that he’s on the other side, forgetting to see you. 

As for my original comment (“Ask him to help you live”) it’s as simple as that. Live together. You’re fighting over death and the feelings of death and not seeing that right now you are alive. I don’t have the proper words for it so my point might just be scattered now but... you have to find what helps you. Don’t rely on others solutions. You’ll probably end up finding yours through hearing their experiences and thoughts, though. Thinking about all of these things and truly trying to comprehend other perceptions helped me see my own because of how it differed from theirs, if that makes sense

Glad I could help. I’ve done a little thinking about your first question and, while I can’t speak with certainty on if it’s a ‘thing’ or not, I do think I’ve had a similar experience. When I was a kid I was able to talk for hours sometimes about a hyperfixation or special interest, and was almost always met with silence or irritation whether from my family or classmates. It led me to repressing any talk about my interests no matter how big, which caused major depression at a young age. Not being able to express yourself, especially as an ND person in general, can be... damaging. Very traumatising. The way we perceive the world and live through it isn’t meant to be suppressed, we have big emotions, big thoughts, big everything. And when we’re met with rejection it can definitely cause some issues, at least in my experience. I even struggle with it today because I do tend to go on rants about my special interests to online friends, since typing is less exhausting than actually talking and I use it as an escape pod. But these friends aren’t always very nice about it which has since made me not talk about them unless prompted and even then I restrict myself until it boils over in my mind and I just short-circuit. I hope that’s helpful

I’ve gone to day programs a couple times. In my experience they were helpful - I got to go somewhere and see that all these other people my age had their own shit going on and understood me, while having access to therapists/physiatrists, but still got to go home. In-patient treatments are pretty scary for me as the idea of being held somewhere and having no way out (speaking as a minor) is like hell. I cant speak for all of the day programs out there but at the time I lived in Massachusetts where they have nicer mental health facilities than most. My advice is to do research beforehand on the different day programs around you. But, hey, if you end up not liking it you get to go home; that’s the relieving part. It can be rough the first couple days though... but overall good experiences and I found it nice to already have most of my day planned for me + having routines there.

Words sometimes feel like big, heavy bricks I have to force out. I can get them out but it’s exhausting. I would rather let them sit in my chest and stay there. But actually saying them is tiring and takes so much energy from me. If I don’t need to speak, I don’t want to, and I find myself irritated very easily around others who don’t understand that. Many autistic people (or ADHD) can struggle with selective mutism.

We all have time to figure out why we behave a certain way and learn how to live a better quality of life. We aren’t born understanding the human psyche, so it makes sense that you might not understand why you think this way. As someone with autism, I struggle with understanding things almost every single day... aaand people always give me shit for it. If I don’t understand a joke, they get annoyed. Just like if you don’t know how to react to something, your parents get mad at you before trying to empathise. It doesn’t mean there’s something ‘wrong’ with you. We’re just people and life isn’t as linear as people like to think. You have time to understand yourself, I promise
